article_title: Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations
citation: Malmberg, J., Haataja, E., & Järvelä, S. (2022). Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09320-z
title: Qridi platform with 6Q tool for situational task perception ratings
description: The Qridi® platform was used to coordinate students' collaborative learning and hosted the 6Q tool, "which was tailored to increase the students’ awareness of collaborative learning and to support their awareness of the regulation of learning". It collected single-item slider ratings (0–100) of task understanding and task difficulty before and after each collaborative task, plus quizzes, with all activities time-stamped on an external server. In this study the information was shown only to students.
requirements: Students rate task understanding and task difficulty before and after each collaborative task using single-item slider scales to minimize interference with group interaction
constraints: In this study the information was offered only to the students, not to the teacher
target_learning_goals: physics content on sound, light, lenses and reflection
examples: Students rated 'How well do you understand the task?' and 'How difficult is the task?' before and after each of five collaborative physics tasks, then completed a five-to-six question multiple choice quiz
key_sources: Malmberg, J., Haataja, E., & Järvelä, S. (2022). Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09320-z

article_title: Quick response-code linked video-based objective structured practical examination: Bridging gaps in pharmacology education.
citation: Eldhose Anupa, Mathew Rohini Ann, Kumar Aniket, Shanthi Margaret. (2026). Quick response-code linked video-based objective structured practical examination: Bridging gaps in pharmacology education. Indian Journal of Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.4103/ijp.ijp_1351_25
title: QR-code-linked OSPE demonstration video resource
description: A set of five self-created videos (6–7 min each) demonstrating IV, IM, SC, and MDI with and without spacer techniques, each with two parts: equipment overview and "a step-by-step demonstration of the skill following a prevalidated structured checklist." Videos were peer-validated, linked with instructional sheets to a QR code, and uploaded to Google Drive for student access two months after baseline teaching.
requirements: Videos must be reviewed and validated by experts before release
Availability of adequate space, equipment, and repeated practice to create clear instructional videos
constraints: Creating OSPE videos requires a significant amount of time, effort, and preparation
target_learning_goals: Correct technique for administering injections via IV, IM, and SC routes
Using a metered dose inhaler with or without a spacer
examples: Videos were recorded using a high-end camera phone by a faculty member, demonstrated by a postgraduate student with a faculty voice-over
key_sources: Eldhose Anupa, Mathew Rohini Ann, Kumar Aniket, Shanthi Margaret. (2026). Quick response-code linked video-based objective structured practical examination: Bridging gaps in pharmacology education. Indian Journal of Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.4103/ijp.ijp_1351_25

article_title: Using active learning methodologies to teach sequence analysis and molecular phylogeny.
citation: Ortiz Martín I, Del Espino Pérez Á, García Luque E, Viguera Mínguez E. (2025). Using active learning methodologies to teach sequence analysis and molecular phylogeny. Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/bmb.21861
title: QR-collection gymkhana combining Problem Based Learning and Game Based Learning with authentic bioinformatics problem solving
description: A lesson-level pattern in which student teams collect 8 QR-encoded protein sequences scattered around the campus botanical garden and use them as starting material for a bioinformatics study. The article states "The active learning methods Problem Based Learning (PBL) and Game Based Learning (GBL) have been chosen as training strategies in this intervention proposal." Students then run BLAST identification, ortholog searches, sequence alignments and phylogenetic tree construction, and write an individual scientific report, with teachers acting as facilitators rather than lecturing.
requirements: Students must have access to molecular databases, BLAST and Seaview in a computer science classroom
Teams require a map of the sampling area and a QR reader; theoretical content must be taught in course lectures beforehand
constraints: The activity spans two non-consecutive days for groups of about 20 students, with approximately 160 students per year divided into eight groups
target_learning_goals: Multiple sequence alignment and phylogenetic tree construction
examples: Teams named Asia, America, Africa and Oceania were each assigned one protein (SDHA, MT-ATP6, MT-CYTB, MT-ND4) marked by a distinct QR-code shape
key_sources: Ortiz Martín I, Del Espino Pérez Á, García Luque E, Viguera Mínguez E. (2025). Using active learning methodologies to teach sequence analysis and molecular phylogeny. Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/bmb.21861

article_title: Smartphone education improves embarrassment, bowel preparation, and satisfaction with care in patients receiving colonoscopy: A randomized controlled trail.
citation: Wen MC, Kau K, Huang SS, Huang WH, Tsai LY, Tsai TY, Tsay SL. (2020). Smartphone education improves embarrassment, bowel preparation, and satisfaction with care in patients receiving colonoscopy: a randomized controlled trail. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000023102
title: QR-code smartphone education program for colonoscopy preparation
description: A multimedia education program delivered by scanning a QR code, covering colorectal cancer information, possible embarrassment situations, bowel preparation, and colonoscopy procedures. It took about 12 minutes, was designed by a multidisciplinary team, was pilot tested with 30 cases, and patients were encouraged to review the content as many times as they needed. It supplemented, not replaced, traditional pamphlet and verbal instruction.
requirements: Patients must own a smartphone and be literate; the program required institutional review and approval by the Medical Administrative Office
constraints: The study could not track how many times patients actually viewed the video, so the dose-response of reviewing remains untested
target_learners: Adult colonoscopy patients in a Taiwanese medical center
target_learning_goals: Understanding colonoscopy procedures and bowel preparation
examples: In the RCT, the smartphone group scanned a QR code to access the program and could review it without limits of place and time
key_sources: Wen MC, Kau K, Huang SS, Huang WH, Tsai LY, Tsai TY, Tsay SL. (2020). Smartphone education improves embarrassment, bowel preparation, and satisfaction with care in patients receiving colonoscopy: a randomized controlled trail. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000023102
